analysis.one_liner: Replaces the graduated income tax with a flat 20 percent tax on wages and business income and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act of 2009, which would have replaced the income tax with a single 20 percent rate and repealed the estate tax, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have scrapped today's graduated income tax and replaced it with a single 20 percent tax on wages, salaries, and business profits, with only a large standard deduction, a charitable deduction, and a home-mortgage-interest deduction. Two things stand out: it would tax only earned income, so investment income like capital gains and dividends would go untaxed at the individual level, and it would repeal the estate and gift taxes entirely. It would also eliminate the public financing of presidential campaigns and the federal program that funds coal miners' health benefits. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners would be high earners and investors: only wages and professional fees would be taxed, so income from investments — capital gains, dividends, interest — would face no individual tax at all. Heirs of large estates would benefit from the full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes. Lower- and middle-income wage earners would see their tax bills fall thanks to the large standard deduction, and everyone would gain from a much simpler filing process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: It cuts the individual rate to a single 20 percent on wages after a generous standard deduction ($12,500 single, $25,000 joint, plus $6,250 per dependent), which would reduce or eliminate federal income tax for many lower- and middle-income wage earners.

It simplifies filing dramatically by replacing the graduated rate structure and most itemized deductions with a single rate and three deductions: the standard deduction, cash charitable gifts (capped at $3,125), and home mortgage interest (capped at $125,000 of debt).

Businesses would pay a flat 20 percent on active business income after deducting inputs, wages, and equipment, with lobbying and political spending made non-deductible — a rare provision that would make companies pay tax on money they spend lobbying.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on public revenue and on whoever must make up the difference: repealing taxes on investment income and estates, while cutting the top rate to 20 percent, would shift more of the tax burden toward wage income and likely require either spending cuts, other tax increases, or more borrowing. Retired coal miners would lose a dedicated health-benefits funding stream, and the public campaign financing system would lose its funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners and retired coal miners

drawbacks.text: It repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely, letting the largest inheritances pass untaxed.

Individuals would pay tax only on wages, salaries, and professional fees — investment income such as dividends, interest, and capital gains would face no individual tax, while the existing top rate of 35 percent on high earners would fall to 20 percent.

It repeals the financing of public presidential election campaigns and the coal industry health benefits provisions, ending a source of coal miners' retiree health coverage funding without a stated replacement.

A revenue-neutral-looking flat rate is not demonstrated; replacing the graduated income tax and estate tax with a 20 percent flat tax would likely shift a larger share of the tax burden onto wage earners unless spending were cut sharply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real: a single rate with few deductions would make filing far easier and eliminate a code riddled with special provisions. But the bill pays for that simplicity by exempting all investment income from individual tax, repealing the estate and gift taxes outright, and eliminating the progressive rate structure — the largest benefits flowing to the highest earners and to heirs of large estates. Meanwhile it repeals the coal miners' health benefits trust fund financing and public campaign financing without replacement. On balance the costs to ordinary taxpayers and to public programs outweigh the simplicity gain, and the bill was so lightly supported that it was never seriously pursued.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Specter introduced the bill on March 30, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No senator joined as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current tax structure stayed in place. Wealthy households kept the progressive rates and the estate tax that this bill would have repealed, so the outcome preserved the existing distribution of the tax burden. Nothing was lost or gained for working people.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the tax code stayed as it was

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2009 and delivered introductory remarks; it was his only action on the measure.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican senator with no cosponsors and drew no recorded support or opposition; party positions were never tested in a vote.

industries.note: The bill taxes only wages and professional fees, leaving dividends, interest, and capital gains untaxed at the individual level, and cuts the top rate from 35 percent to 20 percent. It also repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes outright.

industries.industry: Large business owners and pass-through enterprises
industries.note: Business income is taxed at a flat 20 percent after deducting inputs, wages, and equipment, with no separate corporate/shareholder layer — a large cut from the 35 percent corporate rate for profitable firms. The one offset is losing deductions for lobbying and political spending.

industries.industry: Coal industry retirees and their health funds
industries.note: The bill repeals the subtitle financing coal industry health benefits, ending a funding mechanism for retired miners' health coverage.
It repeals the tax provisions that fund presidential election campaigns, removing that public financing mechanism.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning industries
industries.note: A radically simplified tax code with one rate and few deductions would shrink the market for complex tax planning and preparation. The bill died, so the effect never materialized.
